title: How do you keep your game's story and lore consistent? (5-min survey for a student research project)
author: Ciyaz
selftext:
Hey guys. I'm a student doing my masters in Digital Media, researching how game teams keep track of their story and lore over a long project, especially when there's a lot of text or more than one writer.

If you've written or edited dialogue, quests, or lore for a game (professional, indie, or hobby), I'd really appreciate 5 minutes of your time:

[https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSecVqA\_o0jvkS7ghM4IIkqvLLxShlIGKH4ezEU3yV9DsLnj2Q/viewform](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSecVqA_o0jvkS7ghM4IIkqvLLxShlIGKH4ezEU3yV9DsLnj2Q/viewform)

It's anonymous, it's for a class project, and nothing is being sold. There's an optional spot at the end if you'd be open to a short follow-up chat. I'll post the results in about two weeks.

Cheers.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
A lot of those survey questions are about continuity.

...I feel like this is a misunderstood issue: continuity errors CAN happens because of genuine mistakes and/or a story just having too many loose strings for the author(s) to tie-off, but most often they happen for a reason that can't be fixed: 

The author and the reader are always going to have different opinions on what matters in a story. A given beat might be something the author considers incidental, so of course it goes 'unresolved' because they didn't think the reader would care. When the reader DOES care about that beat, that becomes a continuity error for them because their expectations aren't aligned with the author's.

That's an unavoidable part of the craft.

A machine that interrogates that author about these things would be very interesting to me and might be useful in terms of offering a different perspective on a manuscript while it is still being written... but it still won't solve the disconnect because nothing can. Suppose I have a beat that involves a character I as the author don't care about. That character, to me, is a means to an end. Normally, they would vanish after that beat and you'd never again hear about them. 

Suppose the AI flags this and I say, 'Oh, okay, fair point," and I include a brief scene where that character is killed or gets on a plane to Istanbul or goes to prison or whatever. 

You as a reader who became invested in a character I didn't think anyone would care about are not going to be happy with this outcome even though it is technically not a continuity error anymore. So we've addressed the 'problem', but not the actual unwanted experience.
